# PLAN: lm, bootstrap residual standard error to find upper bound for model error, print 5 dropdown answers
library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
df_clean <- fairs %>%
  mutate(cost = as.numeric(as.character(cost)), visitors = as.numeric(as.character(visitors))) %>%
  drop_na(cost, visitors)
set.seed(123)
boot_err <- do(1000)*sigma(lm(cost ~ visitors, data = resample(df_clean)))
ci_up <- quantile(boot_err$result, 0.975)
opts <- c(26, 870, 430, 66, 50, 1100)

# PLAN: bootstrap, Age ~ ConsiderFan, franchise data
library(mosaic)
set.seed(42)
boot_diff <- do(5000) * diffmean(Age ~ ConsiderFan, data = resample(franchise))
ci <- confint(boot_diff)
pt_diff <- diffmean(Age ~ ConsiderFan, data = franchise)
print(pt_diff)
print(ci)
mean_by_group <- mean(Age ~ ConsiderFan, data = franchise)
print(mean_by_group)

# Determine the answers for the blanks
# Blank 1: younger / older (Are Yes respondents older or younger than No respondents?)
# Blank 2: value (diff rounded)
# Blank 3: generalizable / not generalizable
# Blank 4: does not contain zero / consists of both positive and negative numbers
# Blank 5: at least approximately X years older/younger (lower bound of interval for No vs Yes)

ans1 <- if(mean_by_group["Yes"] < mean_by_group["No"]) "younger" else "older"
diff_val <- round(abs(mean_by_group["Yes"] - mean_by_group["No"]))
# let's find the closest option among 4, 45, 1, 49, 6
options_diff <- c(4, 45, 1, 49, 6)
closest_diff <- options_diff[which.min(abs(options_diff - abs(pt_diff)))]

sig <- if(ci$lower > 0 || ci$upper < 0) "generalizable" else "not generalizable"
contain <- if((ci$lower > 0 && ci$upper > 0) || (ci$lower < 0 && ci$upper < 0)) "does not contain zero" else "consists of both positive and negative numbers"

cat("Blank 1:", ans1, "\n")
cat("Blank 2:", closest_diff, "\n")
cat("Blank 3:", sig, "\n")
cat("Blank 4:", contain, "\n")
cat("Blank 5:", paste(closest_diff, "years"), "\n")
cat("CONFIDENCE: High\n")

failures.question: This question revisits the data on video-game reaction time that we analyzed in class and in Lesson 14. Specifically, we'll consider three variables from this data set (two that we looked at before, and one that we didn't): PictureTarget.RT: the subject's reaction time in milliseconds when presented with a visual stimulus FarAway: a dummy variable for whether the stimulus (i.e. the “bad guy” popping up on the screen) was near (0) or far away (1) within the visual scene. SceneLetter: a letter code (b, c, d, e, or f) indicating which of five scenes the subject was presented with. (Note: the scene letters start at b; there is no scene a in this data set) Consider the following model and its corresponding regression table: lm(PictureTarget.RT ~ FarAway + SceneLetter + FarAway:SceneLetter, data=rxntime) %>% get_regression_table() %>% select(-std_error, - statistic, - p_value) Based on this regression table, which of the following statements is accurate? (1) This model includes an interaction term for the FarAway and SceneLetter variables. (2) The interaction of SceneLetter: d and a FarAway stimulus implies some decrease in reaction time (with 95% confidence) after accounting for the main effects. (3) If the stimulus is FarAway and the interface shows SceneLetter: a , we expect a slower reaction time by approximately 20-75 milliseconds with 95% confidence.
